Splunk Enterprise / Search Tutorial

From raw events to a useful dashboard.

A plain-language companion to the Splunk Enterprise 10.6 Search Tutorial. You’ll load a small fictional shop’s data, find patterns, add product names, and turn useful searches into reports and dashboards.

This guide uses original explanations and exercises rather than reproducing Splunk’s wording. The official pages remain the authority for release-specific interface details and installation requirements. UI labels can differ slightly between Splunk Cloud and Enterprise.

Before you begin: Use a trial or a non-production instance. The exercises upload sample data and create saved knowledge objects. Keep the original ZIP files intact until the upload step asks for them.

Practice dataset Buttercup Games — fictional web access, sales, and product-price data.

Part 01 · Preparation

Get a working Splunk instance

Choose Splunk Cloud Platform or Splunk Enterprise. Cloud runs in a browser; Enterprise is installed on a supported host. This walkthrough assumes an account with permission to upload data and create searches, lookups, reports, and dashboards.

Set up checklist

  1. Create or sign in to your Splunk account and start the appropriate trial.
  2. For Enterprise, install the package for your operating system, create an administrator login, and start the service. Treat the password as a credential—don’t put it in notes or this guide.
  3. Open Splunk Web. A local Enterprise install commonly uses http://localhost:8000; Cloud uses the instance URL provided to you.
  4. Download the official tutorialdata.zip and Prices.csv.zip. Keep both compressed for now.

Enterprise Linux start example (adjust the install directory to yours):

cd <Splunk_Enterprise_Installation_Directory>/bin
./splunk start
# common service controls:
./splunk status
./splunk stop
./splunk restart

Windows installs can start from the Start menu or Services; macOS/Linux steps and supported versions are release-specific. Check Splunk’s current installation manual before installing.

Find your way around

Splunk Home lists apps. Open Search & Reporting to work with searches. The global Splunk bar is the route back home and to account, settings, and system messages. In the Search app, the app bar navigates among Search, Reports, Alerts, and Dashboards.

Install and launch (Enterprise)

On Windows, run the MSI, accept the license, create the Splunk administrator credentials, and finish the installation. On Linux, install the matching RPM/DEB or unpack the TAR package, then start Splunk from its bin directory. On macOS, use the package instructions for the supported release. First startup asks you to accept the license and establish a Splunk admin account. Open Splunk Web at the host’s configured web port (default 8000 for a local install) and sign in with the Splunk account you created during setup—not your OS or splunk.com credentials.

Cloud users skip local installation and sign in to the trial instance URL. From Home, open the Search & Reporting app. Account/settings labels vary by platform; Cloud may show “Splunk Administrator,” while a new Enterprise instance commonly shows “Administrator.”

Part 02 · Ingestion

Bring in the practice data

Splunk turns incoming records into searchable events. During indexing, it recognizes timestamps and extracts useful structure; the records are stored in an index (often main by default). Buttercup Games data includes web access requests, security logins, and vendor sales rows. The sample ZIP is generated with a recent seven-day timestamp window when downloaded, so a file downloaded earlier may need a wider search window.

  1. In Settings, choose Add Data, then Upload.
  2. Select tutorialdata.zip from your downloads. Keep it compressed; the compressed upload is recognized and skips the manual source-type selection screen.
  3. Continue to Input Settings. For the tutorial archive, set Host to Segment in path and segment number 1; leave the other prescribed settings unchanged unless your course version instructs otherwise.
  4. Review, submit, then select Start Searching. Confirm that the automatically run search returns events.
  5. Keep Prices.csv.zip for the lookup exercise. Unzip that one later; it contains prices.csv.
Checkpoint: Data can be present but invisible to your current search if the time range is too narrow, the index differs, or your role lacks access. Confirm the upload status and widen the time picker before troubleshooting further.

Raw access lines become fields such as client IP, timestamp, product ID, and HTTP status. Secure events include authentication outcomes; vendor sales rows carry vendor/account identifiers and product codes. This is why searching is more useful than opening a large raw log file.

Part 03 · Orientation

Read the Search app

Start in Search & Reporting. The search bar holds your SPL query; the time picker limits the time window; Search runs it. Search Summary helps you get started, while a results view exposes the data returned by your query.

Event searches

Use the Events tab to inspect matching raw records. The timeline helps spot bursts over time. The fields sidebar shows extracted key/value fields; pin selected fields when they matter to the current task.

Transforming searches

Commands such as stats, top, and chart reshape events into tables or visualizations. Those results appear in Statistics and Visualization rather than as a simple event list.

Search history is useful for revisiting work. Time range and search mode affect what you see and how quickly the search runs. For this tutorial, use SPL examples as written and check the selected language if your deployment offers SPL2.

Set a useful time window

Time filtering is a practical way to keep a search focused. The dataset is historical and spans roughly the week before it was downloaded; it does not necessarily include events from the present day. If the default Last 24 hours returns nothing, try Yesterday, Previous week, Last 7 days, or All time. For a custom relative window, specify an earliest offset (for example, two days ago) and a latest boundary. Use calendar/date-time ranges when you know exact boundaries. Real-time presets are not useful for this static sample.

Search views · Time ranges

Part 04 · Search

Ask questions of events

Begin with a broad term, then narrow with fields and time. The Search Assistant can suggest terms and recent searches, but verify the query and time window before trusting the results.

Find Buttercup errors

Set the time range to All time for the tutorial’s baseline example, then run:

buttercupgames (error OR fail* OR severe)

Adjacent terms imply AND. Parentheses keep the alternatives grouped; fail* matches words beginning with “fail.” Boolean operators are uppercase. Counts can vary if your data, time range, or version differs.

Move from events to answers

  • Events: inspect raw records and timestamps.
  • Fields: narrow on extracted values, such as status, action, or productId.
  • Statistics: use a transforming command to aggregate.
  • Visualization: select a chart that fits the resulting table.

Example progression: search a source type, constrain status/action, then use stats count BY field to compare groups. Keep the time picker intentional; a valid query over the wrong time window can look like a failed query.

Practice: Run a broad search first. Add one condition at a time and compare the event count. This makes mistakes easier to locate than pasting a complicated query all at once.

Search by field

A field query pairs a field name with a value. Names are case-sensitive; values generally are not. Use quotes when a value contains spaces, and a wildcard when a family of values is intended. For example, this selects web access events:

sourcetype=access_*

Fields such as clientip, status, action, and categoryId let you ask narrower questions. The Fields sidebar distinguishes selected fields (shown with events) from interesting fields (frequently present in the matching set). Promote useful fields so they are visible while inspecting results.

Use SPL as a pipeline

A pipe sends the results on its left into the command on its right. The Search Assistant can suggest commands as you type. To inspect the most common purchase category:

sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase | top categoryId

To find the most frequent purchasing client and summarize that client’s purchases in one search, place a focused subsearch in square brackets. Splunk evaluates that inner search first and uses its returned field/value as a condition for the outer search:

sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase
[ search sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase
  | top limit=1 clientip | table clientip ]
| stats count AS "Total Purchased",
        dc(productId) AS "Unique Products",
        values(productId) AS "Product IDs" BY clientip

Compare this with running two separate searches: a subsearch keeps the “top client” step attached to the summary, so the answer updates with the selected time range. Keep subsearches focused and bounded.

Part 05 · Enrichment

Add meaning with a lookup

Events may contain a product ID but not a readable product name. A CSV lookup maps one value to another, adding human context without rewriting the original event.

Prepare the lookup

  1. Unzip Prices.csv.zip so you have prices.csv. Avoid opening and resaving it in a spreadsheet program, which can alter formatting.
  2. In Settings → Lookups, upload the CSV to the Search app and name it prices.csv.
  3. Set file permissions only as broadly as the exercise requires. Global sharing makes it available across apps; consider whether that is appropriate in your environment.
  4. Create a file-based lookup definition named prices_lookup pointing to prices.csv.
  5. To automate enrichment, create an automatic lookup for sourcetype access_combined_wcookie, matching lookup productId to event productId. Map product_name to output field productName, and optionally map price to price.

Use a lookup explicitly in a search when you want to control where enrichment happens. An automatic lookup applies based on the configured sourcetype. Check permissions and field mappings if the new fields do not appear.

sourcetype=access_combined_wcookie
| lookup prices_lookup productId OUTPUT product_name AS productName price

This is a generic validation pattern; confirm the dataset fields and lookup behavior in your instance before using it in later reports.

After enabling the automatic lookup, search sourcetype=access_* and promote price and productName from Interesting to Selected fields. Then create a readable product/price table:

sourcetype=access_* | stats values(price) AS Price BY productName
| rename productName AS "Product Name"

For the VIP summary from Part 4, change the aggregated value from product IDs to names with values(productName). An event without a matching product ID will not gain lookup fields—that is expected.

Important dependency: The following reporting exercises rely on the product lookup being configured. If product names are missing, fix the lookup before building reports.

Part 06 · Reporting

Save a search as a report

A report is a saved search with a name, description, and optional time control. Start with a working query and a useful time range, then save it so it can be revisited or shared.

The official tutorial’s VIP-customer exercise aggregates purchase events by client IP. Its search is reproduced here as a runnable example for the supplied tutorial data:

sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase
[ search sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase
  | top limit=1 clientip
  | table clientip ]
| stats count AS "Total Purchased",
        dc(productId) AS "Total Products",
        values(productName) AS "Product Names" BY clientip
| rename clientip AS "VIP Customer"

Run it over Last 7 days first; if the result is empty, expand the window. Save As → Report, use a clear title and description, and enable a time range picker if viewers should change the period. New reports are typically private. Adjust sharing deliberately and grant only the access needed.

Charts are choices, not decoration

Use a chart when it makes a comparison or trend clearer than a table. The result fields determine which chart types fit. Validate labels, units, time span, and the underlying statistics before saving or sharing.

Build and tune the tutorial charts

Use a transforming search to compare product actions. The chart command builds columns for views, adds-to-cart, and purchases:

sourcetype=access_* status=200
| chart count AS views
  count(eval(action="addtocart")) AS addtocart
  count(eval(action="purchase")) AS purchases BY productName
| rename productName AS "Product Name", views AS Views,
  addtocart AS "Adds to Cart", purchases AS Purchases

Review the Statistics table first, then choose a column chart when comparing several measures across products. The overlay lesson adds conversion rates with eval and puts the percentage lines on a second axis so counts and percentages are not mixed on one scale. Rotate crowded product labels and title both axes before saving.

For purchase trends over time, use timechart and omit null/other product buckets when appropriate:

sourcetype=access_* | timechart count(eval(action="purchase")) BY productName usenull=f useother=f

For compact per-category trends, add a sparkline:

sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase
| chart sparkline(count) AS "Purchases Trend" count AS Total BY categoryId
| rename categoryId AS Category

Save these as reports with clear titles, descriptions, and time-range controls. The official tutorial names the examples “Product Purchases over Time” and “Purchasing trends.” Sharing defaults to private; grant app-level read access only when appropriate. Reports can also be opened for editing, cloned, scheduled, or inspected for properties.

Part 07 · Dashboards

Bring the useful pieces together

A dashboard is a collection of panels. Each panel can show a chart, table, or other view, often backed by a saved report. A good dashboard answers a specific question quickly rather than collecting every chart you have made.

  1. Start with a saved report or search visualization that already answers one clear question.
  2. Choose Save As and add it as a dashboard panel, or create a dashboard and add panels in the editor.
  3. Give the dashboard and panels descriptive names. Place the most important summary first.
  4. Check that the time range and field labels make sense to someone who did not build the search.
  5. Set dashboard permissions intentionally. Test viewing as an intended audience where possible.

When the built-in editor cannot express a needed layout or behavior, the dashboard configuration offers more advanced controls. Treat configuration edits as a separate, tested change: keep a copy and validate the dashboard after each edit.

Create the first panel

Run a successful-purchase search and rank categories, then save its visualization as a new private dashboard named Buttercup Games - Purchases. Start the panel as a pie chart for category share. The dashboard editor can add panels from new searches, saved reports, or another dashboard; drag panels into a useful reading order.

sourcetype=access_* status=200 action=purchase | top categoryId

Add a shared time input

Add a Time input, give it a meaningful label and token (the tutorial uses BG_Purchases_Time_Range), and choose a useful default such as Previous week. An input does not automatically control every panel: bind an ad hoc-search panel to the shared time picker in that panel’s search settings. A panel based on a saved report may not accept that shared picker in the same way; review the panel source and report scheduling behavior.

Finish the dashboard

Add the saved “Purchasing trends” sparkline report and the action/conversion comparison report. Add the VIP client purchase search as another panel, then arrange the panels so the category summary and important comparisons are easy to scan. Save and test the dashboard, its time control, and its visibility permissions. Keep it private until you intend to share it.
